title: Bava Metzia 59b: The Oven of Akhnai and Wronging with Words
bigQuestion: When a majority wins an argument, what does it owe the person who lost?

story.title: Heaven Laughs
story.kicker: A rabbi meets the prophet Elijah and asks what God did on the day the sages outvoted a miracle.
paragraphs: The story is told in the Babylonian Talmud, Bava Metzia 59b. Rabbi Nathan, a sage of the second century, is walking when he meets Elijah the prophet. In rabbinic stories Elijah often appears to sages and answers their questions. Rabbi Nathan has a question about a famous quarrel in the house of study.

The quarrel was about an oven. Rabbi Eliezer said the oven was ritually pure. The other sages said it was impure. Rabbi Eliezer brought every argument he had. When they did not accept them, he called on a carob tree, a stream and the walls of the study house to prove him right. Each one moved. Then a voice from heaven agreed with him.

Rabbi Joshua stood up and quoted Deuteronomy: it is not in heaven. The sages ruled against Rabbi Eliezer anyway. So Rabbi Nathan asks Elijah what God did in that hour. The Gemara gives Elijah's answer: God smiled and said, My children have defeated me, my children have defeated me.

But the story does not end with a smile. The sages burn the things Rabbi Eliezer had called pure, and they ban him. A great teacher weeps. Harm follows in the world, and a leader dies. The Gemara tells all of this inside a chapter about hurting people with words. This chapter reads the whole passage and asks why.
story.think: Why might the Talmud place a story about a winning majority inside a discussion of hurting people with words?

lessons.title: A Chapter About Fair Dealing
lessons.mainIdea: Bava Metzia 59b sits inside a chapter about ona'ah, wronging people in trade and in speech.
reading: Bava Metzia means the Middle Gate. It is the middle of three tractates about damages and property. Its fourth chapter deals with ona'ah, a Hebrew word for wronging or cheating. The Mishnah first discusses overcharging: how far a price may stray from fair value before a sale can be undone.

Then Mishnah Bava Metzia 4:10 turns from money to speech. It says that just as there is wronging in buying and selling, there is wronging in words. Its examples are small and sharp. Do not ask a seller the price of something if you have no plan to buy it. Do not say to someone who has changed their ways, remember what you used to do.

The Mishnah also warns against reminding a convert of what their ancestors did. The Gemara that follows gathers teachings on this theme. The oven story comes in the middle of that discussion. So the editors placed it in a chapter whose subject is the harm done by careless or cruel words.

words.d: wronging; in the Talmud, both unfair prices and hurtful words
the first written collection of rabbinic law, edited c. 200 CE
the later rabbinic discussion of the Mishnah that fills most of each Talmud page
one book of the Mishnah or Talmud, named for its subject

lessons.title: Shame Like Shedding Blood
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara treats public shaming as a very grave harm, comparing it to shedding blood.
reading: Just before the oven story, on Bava Metzia 58b, the Gemara reports a teaching heard in the study house. Whoever makes a friend's face go pale in public is like one who sheds blood. The image is physical. When a person is shamed, the red leaves their face and it turns white, as if blood were spilled.

The Gemara piles up related sayings. One says that verbal wronging is worse than cheating in money, because money can be paid back and shame cannot. Another says a person should rather be thrown into a furnace than shame someone in public. The sages who taught these lines were using strong words on purpose.

Readers have taken this passage in different ways. Many Jewish teachers use it in schools and sermons as a rule of daily kindness. Legal writers ask how it applies in business or courts. Either way, it sets the mood for what follows. The oven story is told right after it, and its readers are primed to watch for shame.

words.d: one unit of Talmudic discussion on a single question
a teaching from the era of the Mishnah that was left out of the Mishnah
Jewish law, the practical rulings the rabbis draw from their discussions

look.title: Two kinds of harm
look.text: Case one: a seller overcharges you by a few dollars. Case two: someone mocks you in front of your class. The Gemara on Bava Metzia 58b says the second harm is greater, because money can be returned but lost face cannot.
look.prompt: Do you agree with the Gemara's reasoning? What could repair each harm?

check.q: On Bava Metzia 58b, making someone's face go pale in public is compared to what?
check.why: The Gemara says whitening a friend's face in public is like shedding blood.

check.q: Why does the Gemara say verbal wronging is worse than cheating in money?

check.why: The passage contrasts money, which can be repaid, with shame, which cannot.

check.q: What is a sugya?

lessons.title: The Verses Behind the Rule
lessons.mainIdea: The rabbis ground verbal wronging in Leviticus 25:17 and care for the stranger in Exodus 22:20.
reading: The rabbis ask where the ban on hurtful words comes from. Leviticus 25 has two verses that both say, do not wrong one another. Verse 14 speaks of buying and selling. The Gemara reads verse 17 as a second command, and since money was already covered, it applies this one to words.

This is a typical rabbinic move. The rabbis assume the Torah does not repeat itself for nothing. When a command seems to appear twice, they look for a new meaning in the second one. Here the extra verse becomes the source of a whole field of ethics about speech.

The Gemara also brings Exodus 22:20 about the stranger, the ger. In rabbinic reading, ger usually means a convert to Judaism. The Gemara teaches that someone who wrongs a convert breaks more than one command. Care for the vulnerable, the person without family or standing in the community, is built into the law.

words.d: in the Bible, a stranger living among Israel; in rabbinic reading, often a convert
the rabbinic method of reading meaning out of the details of a biblical verse
the Jewish Publication Society's English Bible of 1917, now in the public domain

look.title: Leviticus 25:17

look.prompt: The Gemara reads this verse as a rule about words. What in the verse's wording supports or resists that reading?

Rabbi Eliezer ruled so at the oven
check.why: The rabbis read a repeated command as adding something new: wronging in words.

check.q: In rabbinic reading, the word ger in Exodus 22:20 often refers to whom?
check.why: Rabbinic interpretation often takes ger to mean a convert.

lessons.title: An Oven in Pieces
lessons.mainIdea: The debate began over whether an oven built from segments with sand between them could become impure.
reading: The Mishnah in tractate Kelim 5:10 describes an oven cut into rings, with sand placed between the pieces. Rabbi Eliezer said such an oven is pure, meaning it cannot receive ritual impurity. The sages said it is impure. The laws of purity mattered for food and for the Temple, and they were studied long after the Temple fell.

Why would the pieces matter? In rabbinic law, a broken vessel is not a vessel and cannot become impure. Rabbi Eliezer may have seen the ringed oven as broken pieces. The sages saw that the plaster or sand bound it into one working oven. Both views have a logic, and the Gemara does not mock either.

The Gemara explains the oven's odd name. Akhnai is related to the Aramaic for snake. The Gemara says the sages surrounded the oven with arguments like a snake coiled around it and declared it impure. The name already hints at a debate that wraps around a person and holds on.

words.d: ritually impure, a status in biblical and rabbinic law, not a sign of dirt or sin
ritually pure
the oven's name; the Gemara links it to the word for snake

check.q: What did Rabbi Eliezer rule about the oven of Akhnai?

check.q: In rabbinic law, what does tamei mean?
check.why: Tamei is a ritual status, not a claim of dirt or sin.

lessons.title: Miracles on Trial
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Eliezer calls on a tree, a stream, the walls and a heavenly voice, and the sages refuse them all.
reading: The Gemara says that on that day Rabbi Eliezer answered every possible argument, and the sages did not accept them. Then he said, if the law is as I say, let this carob tree prove it. The tree was uprooted and moved a hundred cubits; some say four hundred. The sages replied, one does not bring proof from a carob tree.

He asked the stream to prove it, and the water flowed backward. He asked the walls of the study house, and they began to lean. Rabbi Joshua scolded the walls: when scholars argue about law, what business is it of yours? The Gemara says the walls did not fall, in honor of Rabbi Joshua, and did not straighten, in honor of Rabbi Eliezer. They are still leaning, it adds.

Finally a bat kol, a heavenly voice, declared that the law follows Rabbi Eliezer everywhere. Many readers note the humor in the leaning walls. They also note the pattern: each proof is bigger than the last, and each is answered the same way. The question is not whether miracles happen in the story. It is whether they count as legal proof.

words.d: literally daughter of a voice; in rabbinic stories, a voice from heaven
the stories and teachings in rabbinic literature that are not law
an ancient length, roughly the length of a forearm

check.q: What did the sages say after the carob tree moved?

check.q: Why did the walls of the study house stay leaning, according to the Gemara?
choices: Because the sages voted to keep them

check.q: What is a bat kol?

lessons.title: It Is Not in Heaven
lessons.mainIdea: Rabbi Joshua answers the heavenly voice with Deuteronomy 30:12, reading it to mean the law is decided on earth.
reading: When the heavenly voice speaks, Rabbi Joshua stands and says, it is not in heaven. He is quoting Deuteronomy 30:12. In its setting, Moses tells Israel that the commandment is not too far away. It is not up in heaven, so no one needs to climb up and fetch it. It is near, in their mouth and heart.

The Gemara asks what Rabbi Joshua meant. Rabbi Jeremiah explains: the Torah was already given at Mount Sinai, so the sages do not follow a heavenly voice. The Torah itself says to incline after the majority, a rabbinic reading of Exodus 23:2. In the story, the Torah is handed over, and people must now interpret it.

Readers have drawn different lessons. Many Orthodox teachers read it as a statement about the authority of the sages who carry the tradition. Conservative and Reform writers often cite it for the idea that law develops through human interpretation. Academic readers note that the story is told by the rabbis about their own authority, and they study how it builds that claim.

words.d: the verse 'It is not in heaven,' which Rabbi Joshua quotes against the heavenly voice
the principle that a vote of the sages decides the law, read from Exodus 23:2
in rabbinic tradition, the teachings and interpretations passed down alongside the written Torah

lessons.title: My Children Have Defeated Me
lessons.mainIdea: In the story, Elijah reports that God smiled and said, My children have defeated me.
reading: The Gemara now turns to Rabbi Nathan meeting Elijah. Rabbi Nathan asks what the Holy One did in that hour. Elijah says that God smiled and said, My children have defeated me, my children have defeated me. The line is doubled in the text, as if repeated with delight.

The word for defeated, nitzchuni, has been read in more than one way. Many read it as victory: the students won the argument, and the teacher is proud. Some later commentators read it as eternalized, from the same Hebrew root: my children have made me last forever. Both readings are offered in Jewish tradition.

This part of the passage is aggadah, a story rather than a ruling. It describes God as a parent who enjoys being outargued. Readers across Jewish movements quote it to celebrate study and debate. Others warn against reading it alone, because the next lines of the Gemara are not joyful at all.

words.d: the biblical prophet who, in rabbinic stories, visits sages and answers questions
Hebrew for 'they have defeated me'; some read it as 'they have made me eternal'
the stories and teachings in rabbinic literature that are not law

lessons.title: The Ban on Rabbi Eliezer
lessons.mainIdea: After the vote, the sages burn what Rabbi Eliezer called pure and ban him, and Rabbi Akiva carries the news gently.
reading: The Gemara continues. That day the sages brought everything Rabbi Eliezer had declared pure and burned it. They voted to place him under a ban, cutting him off from the community of scholars. Then they asked who would go and tell him. The news had to reach a great teacher, and it would hurt.

Rabbi Akiva, his student, said he would go, so that no unfit person would tell him and destroy the world. Akiva dressed in black and sat at a distance of four cubits, signs of mourning and of the ban. Rabbi Eliezer asked what was different about today. Akiva answered carefully: it seems to me your colleagues are keeping away from you.

Rabbi Eliezer tore his clothes, took off his shoes and sat on the ground, and he wept. Readers notice the gentleness of the messenger and the weight of the moment. The majority won the law, but the story now shows a great teacher in grief. The words of the sages, however right, have wounded a person.

words.d: a ban that separated a scholar from others for a time
a set distance kept from a person under a ban
a leading sage of the early second century and a student of Rabbi Eliezer

look.title: Choosing the messenger

look.prompt: What does Akiva's choice teach about delivering hard news? How does it connect to ona'ah?

check.q: Who volunteered to tell Rabbi Eliezer about the ban?
check.why: Rabbi Akiva, Eliezer's student, carried the news.

check.q: Why did Rabbi Akiva go himself?

lessons.title: Harm in the World
lessons.mainIdea: The Gemara describes damage that follows Rabbi Eliezer's grief, including a storm that threatens Rabban Gamliel.
reading: The Gemara says that after the ban, the world was struck: a third of the olives, a third of the wheat and a third of the barley. Some say even dough in a woman's hands spoiled. Wherever Rabbi Eliezer set his eyes, it burned. The story treats his pain as powerful.

Rabban Gamliel, the head of the academy who had led the ban, was traveling on a ship. A great wave rose to drown him. He said, it seems to me this is because of Rabbi Eliezer. He stood and prayed: you know that I did not do this for my own honor, but for yours, so that disputes would not multiply in Israel. The sea grew calm.

Readers point out that the story takes both sides seriously. Rabban Gamliel's reason is real: a community needs a way to settle law. Yet the story still shows the cost of the ban. It does not say the majority was wrong about the oven. It says that winning does not erase the hurt.

words.d: Rabban Gamliel II, head of the academy at Yavneh in the late first century
the town where sages gathered after 70 CE to rebuild study
a dispute between sages, recorded with both sides

lessons.title: The Gates of Wounding
lessons.mainIdea: Imma Shalom's words close the story: every gate may be locked except the gate of those who are wounded.
reading: The last scene takes place in Rabbi Eliezer's home. His wife, Imma Shalom, was Rabban Gamliel's sister. The Gemara says she did not let her husband fall on his face in the supplication prayer, fearing his prayer of pain would harm her brother. One day, a poor man came to the door, and she went to give him bread.

Rabbi Eliezer fell on his face in prayer. When she returned she said, get up, you have killed my brother. Just then a shofar sounded from Rabban Gamliel's house to announce his death. Rabbi Eliezer asked how she knew. She said she had a tradition from her father's house: all the gates are locked, except the gates of ona'ah.

Now the frame closes. The chapter began with wronging in words and ends with it. Many readers, including the scholar Jeffrey Rubenstein in Talmudic Stories (1999), argue that this ending shows the editors' purpose: the tale is finally about the pain of Rabbi Eliezer's shaming. Others emphasize the teaching about majority rule. The Talmud keeps both in view.

words.d: Rabbi Eliezer's wife and Rabban Gamliel's sister in the Talmud's story
the supplication prayer, said in some settings while leaning forward, 'falling on one's face'
a ram's horn, blown here to announce a death

lessons.title: Authority and Mercy Together
lessons.mainIdea: The passage holds two lessons at once: the majority decides the law, and the one who loses must still be treated with care.
reading: Read quickly, the passage seems to teach one thing: the sages, by majority vote, decide the law. That idea became central in Jewish legal thought. But read in its setting, a second lesson runs alongside. The ban and its cost are told in detail, and the chapter's subject is hurting people with words.

The Talmud often works this way. It does not always say which lesson is the main one. It places them side by side and leaves the reader to weigh them. The minority view of Rabbi Eliezer is not erased either. It remains in the Mishnah in Kelim, named and recorded.

This is where the course's two threads meet. Argument: the story shows how a law is settled, even against a miracle. Mercy: it shows what a community owes the person who loses. A student who reads only one half has missed the other. The editors seem to want readers to hold both.

words.d: a view that lost the vote but is still recorded in the Talmud
the unnamed people who arranged the Talmud's material, often called the stammaim by scholars
the setting around a story that shapes how it is read

lessons.title: How Modern Readers Disagree
lessons.mainIdea: Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and academic readers use the oven story in different ways without one reading replacing the others.
reading: Many Orthodox writers read the story as teaching the authority of the rabbinic tradition. The law is decided by qualified sages through the rules of interpretation. A heavenly voice cannot overturn it. In this view, the chain of teachers carries the Torah faithfully.

Conservative writers have often cited the story to show that Jewish law is shaped by human interpretation over time, within a community of scholars. Reform writers sometimes use it to honor debate and individual conscience, and some point to Rabbi Eliezer as a voice for the one who stands alone. Each movement finds support in the text.

Academic scholars, such as Izhak Englard in a 1975 article and Jeffrey Rubenstein in 1999, study how the story was built and when its parts were added. Some compare it with a shorter version in the Jerusalem Talmud. This course does not choose a winner. It shows how one passage can carry many readings.
